newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Volcano profoundly alters verdant British colony.
newsitem.headline: Volcano profoundly alters verdant British colony.

text.p: In the 19 months since Montserrat's volcano rumbled to life, Marian O'Garro and her children have moved from a comfortable life in a spacious home in the capital to cots in a cramped church shelter.
Her house has collapsed, destroyed by the weight of falling ash, and the government delivers her family's food rations weekly in a cardboard box.
"I think God is teaching us a lesson," she said.

Since it first erupted on July 18, 1995, Montserrat's Soufriere Hills volcano has dramatically changed life in this verdant British Caribbean colony. A constant dusting of ash has people carrying kerchiefs and surgical masks and plates and cups often must be wiped clean before every meal.

The volcano has chased a third of the 11,000 residents to neighbouring islands or back to Britain, sometimes splitting families, rousted hundreds of others from comfortable homes to crowded shelters and hobbled a once-burgeoning economy.

An upscale tourist destination and jet-set hangout -- in the 1980s the likes of Paul McCartney, Elton John and The Police recorded at George Martin's Air Studios -- the island now relies on the largesse of the United Kingdom. Unemployment has risen from five percent to 50 percent and many of the remaining 7,000 people receive public assistance.

Britain has spent nearly $5 million on emergency relief and pledged $40 million in development aid. Prince Andrew, who toured the island this week, pledged continuing support and told Montserratians he would make a written report on his trip to the Foreign Office "to make sure they don't forget you."

Montserrat's spectacular vistas -- lush valleys, sheer cliffs and black sand beaches -- are for the most part untouched by the volcano. But the mountain frequently blasts ash into the air and sends rivers of hot rock and gas down its flanks. Huge areas around the steaming crater are denuded, vegetation seared by rock or smothered by sulphurous gas.
Frequent rains of acidic ash and flows of volcanic rubble have severely damaged Plymouth, the now-abandoned capital, seat of government and heart of the Montserrat community.

The weight of fallen ash has collapsed roofs of buildings and homes shuttered and boarded when Plymouth was evacuated last April 3. Ash drifts three feet (one metre) high against buildings while rain overflowing from a choked drainage channel coats streets with mud.
Plymouth's people have scattered. Some 800 have lived for more than 10 months in cramped public shelters, where septic tanks are overflowing and nerves are wearing thin.

"We don't have any light in our kitchen. We only have one toilet for 15 people," said Celcilia Weekes, a 35-year-old mother of seven who worked as a maid and had her own three-bedroom home. Now she and five of her children share three bunk beds in an aluminum barracks-type shelter that floods when it rains. Privacy is non-existent.
Gov. Frank Savage said the volcano had driven many residents to the brink of poverty because people forced from the danger zone were still paying mortgages on evacuated and damaged homes.
"Many have exhausted their life savings," Savage said. "It is not a rich island and people are suffering."
Devout and stoic, some Montserratians see the volcano's lingering threat as a test; others, a sign of God's anger.
"Life has changed a lot. These are trying times," said O'Garro, a mother of two. "But there started to be divisions between us. The volcano has brought rich and poor together. This is an equaliser."
